interface.name: agora_shell

description.summary: the window server's own window management

interface.description: One global. It hands out the two objects above it: a window, which is what a surface becomes, and an output, which is where the work area comes from.

enum.name: error

description.summary: what this global can refuse

enum.description: A surface has ONE role, and the two role protocols disagree about who decides the size — so a surface that already has one is refused rather than quietly obeying two contradictory models.

entry.name: already_has_role
entry.summary: that surface already has a role

request.name: get_window

description.summary: give a surface the role of a window

request.description: A surface with no role is never composited, so this is what makes a surface a window. It is the counterpart of `xdg_wm_base.get_xdg_surface` and may not be combined with it on the same surface: a surface has ONE role, and the two roles disagree about who decides the size.

request.name: get_output

description.summary: ask an output for its work area

request.description: `wl_output` describes what a screen IS — its geometry and its mode. This describes what is LEFT of it, which is a question only the window server can answer because the answer depends on the furniture the server owns.

interface.name: agora_output

description.summary: an output, and the part of it an application may use

interface.description: A COMPANION TO `wl_output`, not a replacement: that interface is the surface a client needs to draw and this one is the one it needs to place itself.

event.name: work_area

description.summary: the frame minus the menu bar and the Dock

event.description: Apple's `NSScreen.visibleFrame`, in the output's coordinates. Sent when the client binds and again whenever it changes — because the Mac's answer to "the work area changed" is that THE APPLICATION CONSTRAINS ITSELF (`constrainFrameRect:toScreen:`), so the server's job is to say what happened and not to move anybody's window.

event.name: menu_bar_area

description.summary: the part of the menu bar an application's own menus may use

event.description:
**THE ONE NUMBER ABOUT THE MENU BAR THAT AN APPLICATION CANNOT DERIVE, AND THE REASON THIS EVENT EXISTS.** The server owns the bar's STRIP and the SYSTEM MENU at its left. Everything to the right of that square is where an application's own menus go — AND THE APPLICATION DRAWS THEM, because they are its menus. This event says where they may begin and nothing else: what goes in the space, and how wide each title is, is the application's business.
A CLIENT CANNOT WORK THIS OUT FOR ITSELF. The System menu's width is the server's, and it is the sort of number that changes with the system's language, its input methods, or a decision made in `window-server` — so an application that guessed would put its first menu UNDER the System menu the first time that width changed, and nothing would tell it. The work area above cannot carry it either: that is a VERTICAL reserve, and the Mac's `-visibleFrame` starts at x = 0 because the bar spans the whole screen. Two different questions, two different events.
**AND THE COLOUR IS IN THIS EVENT BECAUSE IT IS A PROPERTY OF THE BAR THE SERVER OWNS.** An application's menus sit IN the bar, and menus drawn on a panel of their own colour are a visible SEAM across a surface that is meant to be one thing. The alternative — every client picking a colour that looks close — is how two greys come to differ by four counts and nobody can say which one is right.

interface.name: agora_window

description.summary: a window, placed and sized by its application

interface.description: **THE APPLICATION IS HONOURED.** Every set_ here is a DEMAND the server writes down and acts on, not a request it may refuse or adjust — which is the inversion of `xdg_toplevel` and the whole point of this protocol. The server's share of the Mac's model is the shadow, the work area, and knowing who is in front.

request.name: set_frame

description.summary: where the window is and how big it is

request.description: `NSWindow.setFrame:display:`, position included. The server honours it exactly: it does not cascade, it does not tile, and it does not move a window the application did not move. Constraining a frame to a screen is the APPLICATION's — `constrainFrameRect:toScreen:`, against the work area above — and a server that did it for the application would be doing it without knowing what the application knows.

request.name: set_status_item

description.summary: make this window an item the SERVER places in the status area

request.description: **THE ONE PLACE THE FRAME RULE DOES NOT REACH, AND THE HEADER IS WHY.** `NSStatusItem` declares `length`, `title`, `image`, `menu`, `target`, `action`, `highlightMode` and `view` — AND NO POSITION OF ANY KIND. A position is what an application placing its own item would need and could not have: it does not know what else is in the status bar, so it cannot know where its own item goes. So THE APPLICATION SAYS HOW LONG ITS ITEM IS AND THE SERVER PACKS IT, from the right edge of the menu bar leftwards, in the order the items were made. `set_frame` will not move such a window afterwards, because a status item is in the menu bar by definition. The two sentinel lengths AppKit has (`NSVariableStatusItemLength`, `NSSquareStatusItemLength`) are its own business: it resolves them to a width before asking, since only it knows how wide its view wants to be.

arg.name: length
arg.summary: how wide the item is, in output coordinates

request.name: set_level

description.summary: where the window sits in the stack

request.description: `NSWindow.setLevel:`, an INTEGER and not a member of a fixed set — so a menu window, a status item and the Dock can be ordered against each other and against ordinary windows without this protocol having anticipated any of them. A window with no level set is at the server's normal level.

request.name: raise

description.summary: bring the window to the front of its level

request.description: `NSWindow.orderFront:`. The application asks and the server honours. WHAT THIS DOES NOT SETTLE IS FOCUS: on the Mac that is the user's click together with `makeKeyAndOrderFront:`, and this protocol has no opinion about it yet.

description.summary: send the window to the back of its level

request.name: set_title

description.summary: the window's name

request.description: Which the application draws itself, as it draws its whole frame; the server records it for its own use — the menu bar of the active application, the window menu — and for anything describing windows to a person.

request.name: set_app_id

description.summary: which application this window belongs to

request.description: The Mac's bundle identifier, near enough: what the menu bar is switched by when this window becomes the active one, and what a launcher or a task list groups by.

request.name: set_visible

description.summary: put this window on the screen, or take it off

request.description: **THE DOOR `xdg-shell` DOES NOT HAVE, AND A REAL APPLICATION NEEDS EVERY DAY.** An `xdg_toplevel` is mapped or destroyed, so a client that wants to hide a window must DESTROY it and build another to show it again — and a menu that closes and reopens would make and throw away a surface each time. `-orderOut:` is not an exotic door: it is what every menu, every sheet and every panel does when it goes away.

arg.name: visible
arg.summary: zero takes it off the screen; anything else puts it back

request.name: set_pointer_grab

description.summary: receive the pointer when it is over no surface at all

request.description:
**THE DOOR A POPUP NEEDS, AND THE ONE THING A MOUSE CLICK CANNOT OTHERWISE SAY.** A Wayland compositor sends pointer events to the surface UNDER the pointer and to nobody when the pointer is over the desktop — so a menu could not hear the click that lands outside it, and "click anywhere to dismiss" was not expressible. While this is set, events that would go to NO surface are delivered to THIS one instead, with coordinates relative to it (which may fall outside its frame — that is how the client learns a click was outside).
IT IS A FALLBACK AND NOT A REAL GRAB, ON PURPOSE: a surface under the pointer still receives the event. A menu bar is the reason — the bar is a SEPARATE window from the menu it opened and the pointer must be able to cross back to it to switch menus, so routing EVERY event to the menu would break the one gesture a menu bar is for. `zero` releases it; destroying the surface releases it too.

arg.name: grab
arg.summary: nonzero takes it; zero gives it back

request.name: destroy

description.summary: the window is gone

request.description: Destroys the object. The surface outlives it and may be given another role, as it may under `xdg-shell`.

event.name: close

description.summary: the server is asking the application to close

event.description: NOT the close button — that button is the application's, like the rest of the frame, and it is the application that decides what closing means. This is for the cases the server does know about: the session is ending, or a window manager's own affordance was used.

event.name: work_area_changed

description.summary: the work area this window is on has changed

event.description: The menu bar grew, the Dock moved, a screen went away. THE SERVER DOES NOT MOVE THE WINDOW: the application constrains itself, and this event is what tells it there is something to constrain.

event.name: pointer_global

description.summary: where the pointer really is, in OUTPUT coordinates

event.description:
**THE ONE COORDINATE A CLIENT-SIDE DRAG CANNOT DERIVE FOR ITSELF, AND THE REASON A FAST ONE WENT WRONG.** The title bar is the application's, so the drag is the application's too — but `wl_pointer.motion` reports the pointer RELATIVE TO THIS WINDOW, and a window that is being MOVED makes that a moving target: a hand that outruns the window puts the pointer on the desktop, the relative number chases its own tail, and the corrections COMPOUND. MEASURED: a fast drag moved the window zero pixels before the pointer grab, and hundreds of pixels past the pointer after it.
This is the ABSOLUTE position the relative one was computed from, sent immediately BEFORE it, so a client holding a grabbed point under the pointer can do it with one subtraction that does not depend on where the window happens to be. It is sent with button events too, because a drag's grab point is a button press.
